classes.title: Difference quotient and definition
classes.description: Direct calculation from the limit of the difference quotient—the foundation of everything.

problem.text: Calculate the derivative of \(f(x) = 7\) using the definition by limit of difference quotient.
problem.hint: What happens to \(f(x+h) - f(x)\) when \(f\) is it constant?

answer.text: The derivative of a constant is zero.

proof_from_limit.title: Proof from the limit of the difference quotient

steps.label: Write the difference quotient
steps.explanation: By definition, the derivative is the limit of this ratio for \(h \to 0\).

steps.label: Replace \(f(x)=7\)
steps.explanation: Since \(f\) does not depend on \(x\), also \(f(x+h)=7\). The difference is always zero.

steps.label: Pass to the limit
steps.explanation: The limit of a function constantly equal to 0 is 0, whatever it is \(h\).

proof_from_limit.conclusion: In general, for each constant \(c\): \((c)' = 0\). Intuitively: a constant function never changes, therefore its rate of variation is zero.

solution_steps.label: Identify function
solution_steps.explanation: Constant function: its value is always 7 regardless of \(x\).

solution_steps.label: Apply rule
solution_steps.explanation: The derivative of any constant is 0.

distractors.feedback: Do not substitute h=0: simplify for h≠0 and then take the limit.
The division by the increment h is missing.
The value of the function and its rate of variation do not coincide in general.

problem.hint: Calculate \(f(x+h)\) replacing \(x+h\) instead of \(x\).

answer.text: The derivative is the slope of the line.

proof_from_limit.title: Proof from the limit of the difference quotient

steps.label: Calculate \(f(x+h)\)
steps.explanation: We replace \(x+h\) in the formula \(f\).

steps.label: Calculate the difference \(f(x+h)-f(x)\)
steps.explanation: The terms \(3x\) and \(5\) cancel — remains only the contribution of \(h\).

steps.label: Form the difference quotient
steps.explanation: The ratio is exactly 3 for every \(h \neq 0\).

steps.label: Pass to the limit
steps.explanation: Since the ratio does not depend on \(h\), the limit is simply 3.

proof_from_limit.conclusion: For a line \(y = mx + q\), the derivative is always \(m\) (the slope). This confirms that the derivative measures slope.

solution_steps.label: Differentiate
solution_steps.explanation: The derivative of \(mx+q\) It is \(m\). The constant term disappears.

problem.text: Calculate \(f'(x)\) for \(f(x) = x^2\) using the definition.
problem.hint: Remember: \((x+h)^2 = x^2 + 2xh + h^2\)

answer.text: The derivative of x2 is 2x.

proof_from_limit.title: Proof from the limit of the difference quotient

steps.label: Calculate \(f(x+h)\) developing the square
steps.explanation: We use the square of a binomial: \((a+b)^2 = a^2+2ab+b^2\).

steps.label: Calculate \(f(x+h)-f(x)\)
steps.explanation: The term \(x^2\) cancels with \(f(x)\).

steps.label: Divide by \(h\)
steps.explanation: We collect \(h\) to the numerator: \(h(2x+h)/h = 2x+h\). Valid for \(h \neq 0\).

steps.label: Pass to the limit
steps.explanation: The term \(h\) vanishes, leaving only \(2x\).

proof_from_limit.conclusion: Results: \((x^2)' = 2x\). This is the case \(n=2\) of the general rule \((x^n)' = nx^{n-1}\).

problem.text: Calculate \(f'(x)\) for \(f(x) = x^3\) using the definition.
problem.hint: Development \((x+h)^3\) with the combination of Newton or by product.

answer.text: The derivative of x3 is 3x2.

proof_from_limit.title: Proof from the limit of the difference quotient

steps.label: Development \((x+h)^3\)
steps.explanation: Using a binomial cube (or Newton formula with \(n=3\)).

steps.label: Calculate the difference
steps.explanation: The term \(x^3\) cancels.

steps.label: Divide by \(h\) collecting
steps.explanation: All the terms of the numerator have \(h\) as a factor, therefore division is simple.

steps.label: Pass to the limit
steps.explanation: For \(h\to 0\), terms with \(h\) and \(h^2\) cancel.

proof_from_limit.conclusion: \((x^3)' = 3x^2\). Case \(n=3\) of the rule \((x^n)'=nx^{n-1}\). The scheme is always the same: Newton's binomial produces a dominant term \(nxh^{n-1}\) that survives the limit.

problem.hint: Write \(\frac{1}{x+h} - \frac{1}{x}\) as the only fraction. Remember: to sum fractions you must find the common denominator.

answer.text: The derivative of 1/x is −1/x2.

steps.label: Write \(f(x+h) - f(x)\) as the only fraction
steps.explanation: Common Denominator \(x(x+h)\). To the numerator: \(x-(x+h) = -h\).

steps.label: Divide by \(h\)
steps.explanation: The factor \(h\) to the numerator and the divider \(h\) delete (with \(h \neq 0\)).

steps.label: Pass to the limit
steps.explanation: For \(h \to 0\), \(x+h \to x\), therefore the denominator becomes \(x^2\).

proof_from_limit.conclusion: \((1/x)' = -1/x^2\). Equivalent to writing \(f(x)=x^{-1}\) and apply \((x^n)'=nx^{n-1}\) with \(n=-1\): \(-1 \cdot x^{-2} = -1/x^2\). ✓

proof_from_limit.title: Proof from the limit of the difference quotient

steps.label: Write the difference quotient
steps.explanation: Initial form of the ratio. The problem is that for \(h\to 0\) we have a form \(0/0\).

steps.label: Multiply by the conjugate
steps.explanation: Multiplying by 1 in the form of the conjugate does not change the value, but transforms the numerator into a difference of squares.

steps.label: Simplify numerator
steps.explanation: \((\sqrt{A}-\sqrt{B})(\sqrt{A}+\sqrt{B}) = A-B\). Here. \(A=x+h\) and \(B=x\).

steps.label: Delete \(h\)
steps.explanation: The \(h\) cancels (valid for \(h\neq 0\)).

steps.label: Pass to the limit
steps.explanation: For \(h\to 0\): \(\sqrt{x+h}\to\sqrt{x}\), therefore the denominator \(\to 2\sqrt{x}\).

proof_from_limit.conclusion: \((\sqrt{x})' = 1/(2\sqrt{x})\). Equivalent to \(x^{1/2}\): with the rule \((x^n)'=nx^{n-1}\) we get \(\frac{1}{2}x^{-1/2} = 1/(2\sqrt{x})\). ✓

problem.text: Calculate \(f'(x)\) for \(f(x) = \sin x\), obtaining the result from the limit of difference quotient.
problem.hint: Use the formula of prostaferesi: \(\sin A - \sin B = 2\cos\frac{A+B}{2}\sin\frac{A-B}{2}\).

answer.text: The derivative of sin x is cos x.

proof_from_limit.title: Full proof from the limit

steps.label: Write the difference quotient
steps.explanation: Standard shape.

steps.label: Apply prostaferesi formula
steps.explanation: With \(A=x+h\) and \(B=x\): \(\sin A - \sin B = 2\cos\frac{A+B}{2}\sin\frac{A-B}{2}\).

steps.label: Rewriting the ratio
steps.explanation: We split up \(h\), then we rewrite \(\sin(h/2)/(h/2)\) multiplying and dividing by \(1/2\).

steps.label: Use the remarkable limit \(\lim_{t\to 0}\frac{\sin t}{t}=1\)
steps.explanation: Here. \(t=h/2\to 0\) when \(h\to 0\). The remarkable limit applies.

steps.label: Complete the calculation
steps.explanation: Since cosine is continuous, the limit is simply \(\cos x\).

proof_from_limit.conclusion: \((\sin x)'=\cos x\). The chain sin→cos→(−sin)→(−cos)→sin repeats cyclically when differentiating.

solution_steps.label: Direct result
solution_steps.explanation: Basic formula, obtained using the remarkable limit \(\lim_{t\to 0}\frac{\sin t}{t}=1\).

distractors.feedback: Check the cycle of derivatives and the point where the minus sign appears.
One is not the derivative universal of elementary functions.
Only the exponential coincides with its own derivative.

problem.text: Calculate \(f'(x)\) for \(f(x) = e^x\) using the definition.
problem.hint: Collecting \(e^x\) out and use the remarkable limit \(\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{e^h-1}{h}=1\).

answer.text: The exponential function is equal to its derivative — single property.

proof_from_limit.title: Proof from the limit — self-derivative of ex

steps.label: Write the difference quotient
steps.explanation: Standard shape.

steps.label: Collecting \(e^x\) using \(e^{a+b}=e^a e^b\)
steps.explanation: \(e^{x+h}=e^x \cdot e^h\). The factor \(e^x\) does not depend on \(h\), and therefore factors out of the limit.

steps.label: Use the remarkable limit
steps.explanation: This limit — equivalent to the definition of \(e\) — is a fundamental result. It is demonstrated using the definition of \(e=\lim_{n\to\infty}(1+1/n)^n\).

steps.label: Concluding
steps.explanation: The surprising result: \(e^x\) is her own derivative.

proof_from_limit.conclusion: \((e^x)'=e^x\). It is the only function (less than constant multiplication) with this property, and describes any phenomenon in which the rate of growth is proportional to the magnitude itself (bacterial growth, radioactive decay, compound interests).

solution_steps.label: Result
solution_steps.explanation: Unique property: the exponential function is unchanged for differentiation.

distractors.feedback: Check the cycle of derivatives and the point where the minus sign appears.

steps.label: Pass to the limit — use continuity
steps.explanation: \(g(x+h)\to g(x)\) because \(g\) It is differentiable, therefore Go on. The two relationships tend to \(f'\) and \(g'\).

proof_from_limit.conclusion: \((fg)' = f'g+fg'\). For our exercise: \(f=x^2, g=\sin x \Rightarrow f'=2x, g'=\cos x\).

classes.title: Chain rule \((f\circ g)'=f'(g)\cdot g'\)
classes.description: Differentiating composite functions—the most important and most frequently used rule.

problem.hint: Identify the external function \(u\mapsto \sin u\) and internal function \(g(x)=x^2\).

answer.text: Differentiate the outside evaluated inside, then multiplies by derivative inside.

proof_from_limit.title: Proof of the chain rule from the limit

steps.label: Write the difference quotient of \(f\circ g\)
steps.explanation: Standard shape.

steps.label: Multiply and divide by \(k = g(x+h)-g(x)\)
steps.explanation: If \(g(x+h)\neq g(x)\), i.e., \(k\neq 0\), we can multiply and divide by \(k\). The second factor is the difference quotient of \(g\).

steps.label: Go to the limit: \(h\to 0\) means \(k\to 0\)
steps.explanation: For \(g\) it is continuous, \(h\to 0 \Rightarrow k\to 0\). The first limit is \(f'\) evaluated in \(g(x)\), the second is \(g'(x)\).

proof_from_limit.conclusion: \((f\circ g)'(x) = f'(g(x))\cdot g'(x)\). For \(\sin(x^2)\): external \(f(u)=\sin u \Rightarrow f'(u)=\cos u\), interior \(g(x)=x^2 \Rightarrow g'=2x\). Results: \(\cos(x^2)\cdot 2x\).

solution_steps.label: External and internal identification
solution_steps.latex: f(u)=\sin u,\quad g(x)=x^2 \Rightarrow f'(u)=\cos u,\quad g'(x)=2x

problem.text: Find the equation of tangent line to the graph of \(f(x)=x^3-3x\) at the point \(P=(2,2)\).
problem.hint: The tangent line in \((x_0, f(x_0))\) has equation \(y - f(x_0) = f'(x_0)(x-x_0)\).

answer.text: Slope 9, pass by (2,2).

proof_from_limit.title: Connection with the definition: why the slope is f'(x0)?

steps.label: The slope the secret between \((x_0,f(x_0))\) and \((x,f(x))\)
steps.explanation: This is the slope of the line that unites two points of graph.

steps.label: For \(x\to x_0\), the secret becomes the tangent
steps.explanation: Replacement \(x=x_0+h\), this limit is exactly the definition of \(f'(x_0)\). The derivative is the slope of the tangent.

proof_from_limit.conclusion: The derivative is not just an abstract formula: it is literally the slope of the right touching graph At one point.

solution_steps.explanation: The slope of the tangent at \(P\) is 9.

problem.text: For \(f(x) = x\cdot e^x\), find the stationary points (where) \(f'(x)=0\)) and study the sign of \(f'\) to classify them.
problem.hint: Use the product rule to find \(f'\). Then study the sign of \(e^x(1+x)\) remembering that \(e^x > 0\) Always.

exercises.title: Challenge — points where the tangent is parallel

problem.text: Find all points of \(f(x) = e^x \sin x\) in \([0,\pi]\) where tangent line is parallel to the axis \(x\) (slope zero). Classify each point as maximum or minimum local.
problem.hint: Parallel to the x axis means \(f'(x)=0\). After calculating \(f'\), study the mark around the points found.

answer.text: A stationary point 3π/4, maximum local.

solution_steps.label: Calculate \(f'\) with the product rule
solution_steps.latex: f'(x) = e^x\sin x + e^x\cos x = e^x(\sin x+\cos x)

solution_steps.label: Solve in \([0,\pi]\)
solution_steps.explanation: \(\sin x = -\cos x \Rightarrow \tan x=-1\). In \([0,\pi]\) the solution is \(x=3\pi/4\).

solution_steps.label: Classification: sign of \(f'\)
solution_steps.latex: x<\tfrac{3\pi}{4}: \sin x+\cos x>0 \Rightarrow f'>0; \quad x>\tfrac{3\pi}{4}: f'<0
solution_steps.explanation: The sign changes from + to −: it is a local maximum.

problem.text: If \(C'(100)=12\) and C is measured in euro while q in pieces, what does it mean?

answer.latex: \text{The cost increases approximately 12 euros per additional piece}
answer.text: The sign indicate increase and the unit is euro/pezzo.
